key_facts: **Epidermoid cysts** are the commonest skin cyst: a mobile dermal nodule with a **central punctum**, filled with keratin ('sebaceous cyst' is a misnomer).
**Pilar (trichilemmal) cysts**: about 90% on the scalp, smooth, no punctum, often multiple and inherited.
Most 'infected' cysts are **inflamed** (ruptured keratin), not infected: antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis or systemic features.
Excise electively once inflammation settles (6–8 weeks), removing the whole wall; cosmetic removal is usually not NHS-funded.
Midline dermoids need imaging before surgery; multiple cysts in a child or young adult suggest **Gardner syndrome** (APC).

ul: **Epidermoid (epidermal inclusion) cyst:** the commonest cutaneous cyst. Its wall resembles epidermis/infundibulum and it is filled with keratin (the "cheesy", foul-smelling contents in [Case 3](condition:dermatofibroma)). "Sebaceous cyst" is a misnomer.
**Pilar (trichilemmal) cyst:** the scalp in ~90%. Firm, smooth, no punctum, often multiple and familial (autosomal dominant). It shells out easily.
**Dermoid cyst:** congenital, along embryonic fusion lines. The classic site is the **lateral eyebrow** (external angular dermoid); midline nasal or scalp dermoids may connect intracranially.
**Milia:** tiny superficial keratin cysts: see [Milia](condition:milia).
**Vellus hair cysts / steatocystoma:** small multiple cysts on the chest; steatocystoma multiplex.

sub: Epidermoid cysts: young and middle-aged adults, more men; face, neck, trunk, scrotum.
Pilar cysts: middle-aged women, autosomal dominant tendency.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Most epidermoid cysts arise from occluded hair follicle infundibula. Others come from implantation of epidermis after trauma (palms/soles), acne, or HPV (plantar). **Rupture** releases keratin into the dermis and causes a sterile foreign-body inflammatory reaction. Most "infected cysts" are actually inflamed, not infected.

ul: Occluded follicular infundibulum; implantation of epidermis after injury; acne.
Drugs: isotretinoin, ciclosporin, BRAF inhibitors.
**"It's a blocked sebaceous gland"**: the cyst is lined by epidermis and contains keratin, not sebum.
**"Squeeze it out"**: squeezing ruptures the wall and causes inflammation and scarring.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A cyst is a sac of **epidermis turned inside out**, shedding keratin into its centre.

mech.t: Follicular infundibulum (or implanted epidermis) forms a closed sac in the dermis.
The lining keeps making keratin, which collects as soft 'cheesy' material; the punctum is the blocked opening.
mech.caption: Epidermoid cyst with a central punctum (left) and a ruptured cyst spilling keratin into the dermis with inflammation (right).

mech.t: Keratin released into the dermis causes a sterile **foreign-body** reaction: red, hot and tender without infection.
Any wall left behind regrows, so excision must remove the whole sac.

histo: Epidermoid: stratified squamous lining with a granular layer and laminated keratin. Pilar: no granular layer, compact keratin (trichilemmal keratinisation).

ul: Mobile, dome-shaped dermal nodule, 0.5–5 cm, on the face, neck, trunk or scrotum, with a **central punctum** in many.
Inflamed or ruptured cysts are red, tender and fluctuant. Recurrence follows incomplete wall removal.

**Gardner syndrome** (a familial adenomatous polyposis variant, **APC** gene): **multiple epidermoid cysts**, often atypical sites (face, scalp, limbs) and **appearing before puberty**; **osteomas** of the skull or jaw; dental anomalies (supernumerary or unerupted teeth); desmoid tumours; CHRPE (retinal pigment lesions); and colorectal polyposis with near-100% colorectal cancer risk if untreated.

sub: Multiple epidermoid cysts before puberty, osteomas, dental anomalies, desmoids and colorectal polyposis: refer to genetics or colorectal services.

ul: Clinical. Ultrasound if unsure (helps distinguish lipoma, lymph node or sarcoma).
**Dermoid cysts in the midline (nasal bridge, scalp), or any lesion with a sinus or hair, need imaging (MRI) before surgery** because of possible intracranial extension. This was the course point.

Gardner: refer to genetics or colorectal services. Triggers are multiple cysts in a child or young adult, especially with osteomas, dental anomalies, or a family history of polyposis or young colorectal cancer.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Lipoma (soft, no punctum, lobulated); pilomatricoma (rock-hard, child, see *Other lumps and syndromes*); dermoid; abscess / hidradenitis (flexural, recurrent, sinus tracts); lymph node; BCC with a cystic component; metastasis; on the scalp, pilar cyst vs proliferating trichilemmal tumour (rapidly growing, ulcerating, elderly woman → biopsy).

ul: **Asymptomatic cysts:** reassure. **Cosmetic removal is usually not NHS-funded** (EBI/local policy). Squeezing worsens inflammation and scarring.

**Inflamed (not infected) cyst:** warm compresses; analgesia. A fluctuant cyst may need incision and drainage, which can be done in some GP settings. **Antibiotics only if there is spreading cellulitis or systemic features** (choose per NICE NG141 cellulitis / local formulary). Avoid routine antibiotics for a "red cyst" (antimicrobial stewardship).

**Elective excision once the inflammation settles (6–8 weeks)** removes the entire wall to prevent recurrence. options include standard elliptical excision, or minimal-incision / punch techniques with lower scar burden but slightly higher recurrence. These are clinician-surgeon decisions (knowledge level only; see the [skin surgery](condition:skin-surgery-preop) notes).

**Refer:** suspected dermoid near the midline or orbit (plastics/paediatric surgery, imaging first); suspected Gardner (genetics/colorectal); rapidly enlarging scalp "cyst" in an older person (biopsy); any lump with sarcoma features (see *Lipoma, angiolipoma and Dercum's disease; the sarcoma lump pathway*).

refer.t: Midline lump on the nose, scalp or spine in a child: **imaging before any surgery**.
Multiple cysts in childhood with osteomas or a family history of bowel cancer: consider **Gardner syndrome (FAP)** and refer.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Midline lump on the nose, scalp or spine in a child: **imaging before any surgery**.
Multiple cysts in childhood with osteomas or a family history of bowel cancer: consider **Gardner syndrome (FAP)** and refer.
Inflammation, rupture and abscess; scarring.
Recurrence after incomplete excision.
Malignant change is very rare; a rapidly growing scalp 'cyst' in an older person needs biopsy (proliferating trichilemmal tumour).
Benign; persists unless excised.

pearls: Explain that the smell comes from keratin breakdown, not poor hygiene.
Recurrence after "popping" or drainage is expected because the wall remains.
Isotretinoin, ciclosporin and BRAF inhibitors can provoke milia or epidermoid cysts. Look at the drug history if cysts erupt.

quiz.q: When should you think of Epidermoid, pilar and dermoid cysts (and Gardner syndrome)?
quiz.a: A smooth, round, mobile lump with a central pore (epidermoid), or several firm scalp lumps (pilar).
Keratin-filled sacs lined by epidermis or hair-root sheath; dermoid cysts are embryonic, often at the outer eyebrow.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Reassure; leave alone or excise the whole wall when not inflamed; inflamed cysts usually are not infected (antibiotics only for cellulitis).
Recurrence after incomplete removal; midline nasal or scalp lumps in children (intracranial connection); multiple cysts with osteomas in Gardner syndrome (FAP).

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Midline lump on the nose, scalp or spine in a child: **imaging before any surgery**.
